title: Trial by Trace: Benchmarking AI Agent Harnesses for Reliability and Failure Attribution
content:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence

Title:Trial by Trace: Benchmarking AI Agent Harnesses for Reliability and Failure Attribution
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:LLM agents are increasingly used to solve real-world problems, and their effectiveness depends on both the underlying models and the harnesses that support their operation. However, most existing benchmarks focus on model capabilities and overall agent performance, with limited attention to the evaluation of agent harnesses. To address this gap, we introduce TraceTrial-Bench, which organizes harness reliability into seven components covering context, execution, governance, lifecycle, observability, tools, and verification. We construct 95 expert-level, mechanism-oriented tasks with executable or state-based ground truth to support semantically equivalent comparisons while preserving the native behavior of each harness. We design a Trajectory Tracing (TT) module to capture agent execution traces and introduce a two-layer evaluation framework that separately assesses agent performance and harness reliability. In addition, we design a Multi-source Evidence Acquisition (MEA) module to provide evidence from the agent context, harness, and execution environment for LLM-based evaluation, and develop a Failure Attribution (FA) module that uses explicit mechanism chains to support attribution at the run level. Across 4 harnesses, 9 models, and 95 tasks, our evaluation of 3,420 runs yields macro-averaged harness scores ranging from 59.8% to 72.0%, while 31.1% of runs achieve task success despite failing at least one harness criterion. TraceTrial-Bench provides an auditable and reproducible foundation for comparing agent harnesses, diagnosing their failures, and studying how harness design interacts with model behavior.

report.summary: TraceTrial-Bench is a new benchmark that evaluates AI agent "harnesses" — the scaffolding around LLMs — across seven reliability dimensions, tracing 3,420 runs to score harnesses and attribute failures.
report.background: As LLM agents move from demos to production, the model is only half the story. The surrounding harness — the loop that manages context, calls tools, enforces permissions, handles retries, logs execution and verifies results — determines whether an agent is dependable. Yet most benchmarks (AgentBench, τ-bench, SWE-bench and their descendants) measure end-task success, implicitly crediting or blaming the model while treating the harness as a black box. That makes it hard to answer practical engineering questions: did the agent fail because the model reasoned badly, or because the harness truncated context, exposed a confusing tool schema, or lacked a verification step? Because harnesses differ wildly in architecture and native behavior, cross-comparison is also fraught. TraceTrial-Bench responds by defining harness reliability as a first-class, auditable object of study, separating harness quality from model capability and providing mechanism-level failure attribution rather than a single pass/fail number.
key_points: Seven-part reliability model: The benchmark breaks harness reliability into context, execution, governance, lifecycle, observability, tools and verification. Each component is scored separately, so teams can see whether their agent stack is weak on, say, permission governance or output verification, rather than receiving one opaque aggregate score.

95 mechanism-oriented tasks: Rather than open-ended puzzles, the suite uses expert-level tasks with executable or state-based ground truth. This lets graders check semantically equivalent outcomes across differently designed harnesses while preserving each harness's native behavior — avoiding the fairness problem of forcing every stack into one architecture.

Two-layer scoring plus failure attribution: A Trajectory Tracing module records full execution traces; one layer scores agent task performance, the other scores harness reliability. A Multi-source Evidence Acquisition module feeds context, harness and environment evidence to an LLM judge, and a Failure Attribution module uses explicit mechanism chains to explain failures at the run level.

The headline numbers: Across 4 harnesses, 9 models and 95 tasks (3,420 runs), macro-averaged harness scores landed between 59.8% and 72.0% — no harness was fully reliable. Critically, 31.1% of runs succeeded at the task while still violating at least one harness criterion, meaning success often masks latent fragility.
report.impact: The most consequential finding is the 31.1% gap between task success and harness compliance: outcome-only benchmarks systematically overstate agent readiness. For the AI industry, this argues for shipping agents with trace-level reliability metrics, not just success rates — a shift that favors teams investing in observability, governance and verification layers. For developers, the seven-component taxonomy is immediately usable as a design checklist and a debugging vocabulary; failure attribution turns postmortems from guesswork into mechanism-level diagnosis, and should reduce the classic confusion between "the model is bad" and "the scaffold is bad." For regular users, the practical effect is fewer silent failures — agents that quietly skip verification or exceed permissions while still appearing to complete the task.
report.tools: Watch for TraceTrial-Bench's code and data (linked via arXiv's Code/Data section, likely Hugging Face). To instrument your own stack with comparable traces, try OpenTelemetry's GenAI semantic conventions with Langfuse, Arize Phoenix or LangSmith; run evaluations with Inspect (UK AISI) or promptfoo. For harness comparisons, test LangGraph, OpenAI Agents SDK, AutoGen and CrewAI against τ-bench and AgentBench to see how task-level scores diverge from trace-level reliability.
